Immunity

By Ruben Hayrapetyan

In this chapter

The Immune System

The innate immune system is a general, fast-acting first line of defense against any pathogen. It operates through three mediums: physical, chemical, and cellular. The physical barriers include mucus in the nose, and the skin. The mucus traps microbes before they can enter through the nasal passages, and the skin’s dry, slightly acidic surface makes it hard for bacteria to colonize. As opposed to the physical barriers, which keep pathogens out, the chemical defenses such as stomach acid, tears and sweat kill pathogens that reach the body’s surfaces and openings. For example, stomach acid specifically kills pathogens that are swallowed with food or drinks. Lastly, the innate immune system has cellular defense mechanisms, utilizing cells like macrophages and neutrophils to engulf and destroy pathogens. While fast, these defenses are non-specific and have no memory, and some pathogens have evolved ways to bypass them. For these more complex infections, the adaptive immune system is needed.

The adaptive immune system provides a slower but much more targeted response to specific pathogens. Unlike the innate immune system, the adaptive immune system can take several days to develop upon the first exposure. Moreover, the adaptive immune system retains information about the pathogen for future similar attacks. This is why vaccines inject a harmless form of a pathogen so that the adaptive immune system can develop immunity to it.

The innate and adaptive immune systems’ joint work starts when a pathogen enters the body. When the immune system recognizes a threat, innate immune cells release cytokines (signaling proteins that coordinate the response and alert other immune cells) to the location of the threat. The blood vessels near the infection widen during an immune response so that the fast-acting innate immune system cells reach the site quickly, which also causes redness, warmth, and swelling. While the innate immune system targets what it can, the antibodies and immune cells neutralize or destroy the remaining pathogens and infected cells in a targeted attack. After the attack, anti-inflammatory signals, including cortisol, dampen the immune response, allowing the affected tissue to repair.

Circadian Rhythms in the Immune System

The immune system, while effective at fighting diseases, cannot be on high alert all the time as it would be too taxing for the human body. As a result, the immune system regulates its active hours by surging at night and being less active during the day. Much of this nighttime surge comes from cytokines, the signaling proteins introduced earlier. There is a vast range of cytokines: there are those that are pro-inflammatory, others that reduce inflammation, and some that raise the body’s internal temperature. While not quite a one-to-one correlation, cytokines can be linked to symptoms such as fever, aches, tiredness, and inflammation: some cytokines raise the body temperature and cause fatigue while others make nerves more sensitive. Cytokines are balanced by a hormone called cortisol, best known for its relationship with stress, and one of its roles is to suppress immune activity. Furthermore, cortisol has a distinct circadian rhythm, with its lowest levels of production during the first half of the night and its highest around waking.

This was shown in a study by Petrovsky and Harrison (1998), in which blood samples were taken from participants at intervals throughout the day. Then, the immune response of the blood was activated by introducing bacterial endotoxin (the outer shells of bacteria) and tetanus toxoid (a harmless form of tetanus). Cytokine counts and plasma cortisol were measured throughout the day, with plasma cortisol levels indicating how much the immune system was suppressed and cytokine counts showing how active the immune system was. The counts showed that cytokine production surged at night and in the early morning, which ran inversely to the circadian rhythm of plasma cortisol levels. However, an inverse pattern on its own cannot show which of the two is driving the other. To test this, the researchers then artificially raised plasma cortisol levels in the evening, and the cytokine levels were dulled. This indicated that the cytokine rhythm is dependent on the cortisol rhythm. These nighttime cytokine peaks help explain a common phenomenon called nighttime flares, in which one’s symptoms worsen during the night and in the early morning.

Beyond nighttime flares, this heightened immune activity also influences the effectiveness of vaccines. Since vaccines are generally harmless antigens that are injected into the body to train the immune system to fight against the harmful pathogens themselves, their success depends on how strongly the immune system responds. So, the time at which they are administered also affects their effectiveness. This is especially relevant for older adults, who tend to have weaker immune responses to vaccination. Long et al. (2016) studied patients over the age of 65 at various general practices in the UK, taking blood samples when they received their flu shots and again one month later to measure antibody levels against the vaccine’s flu strains. The trials found that older adults who received their vaccinations in the morning had higher antibody levels than those who were vaccinated in the afternoon. While intuitively this could be attributed to the increased cytokine production in the early morning, and therefore increased immune activity, researchers found that cytokine levels did not account for the difference. The underlying cause of this difference is still a topic of open research. While part of the mechanism is still unknown, this study shows that the immune system’s response to the vaccine depends on the time of day, suggesting a circadian rhythm in its activity.

Despite the generally protective role of the immune system, it is possible, for a large enough threat, to overreact in a poorly controlled manner and to ultimately damage the body’s own cells. This state is called sepsis. For sepsis, the circadian rhythm of the immune system is very consequential. This was highlighted when researchers (Halberg et al., 1960) injected mice with bacterial endotoxin at different times to drive them into a state of sepsis. Since the mice’s cortisol levels were at their lowest during their daytime rest phase, the mice that were injected during the day were at a much higher risk for their immune systems to overreact as opposed to the mice that were injected at night.

Seasonal Rhythms in Immunity

These daily rhythms are not the only cycles that shape immune activity. Over the course of a year, the immune system is also impacted by a longer infradian rhythm that follows the seasons. One way to see this is by following the body’s gene expression as it varies across seasons. Gene expression is how the body controls protein production, reducing the production of some proteins while amplifying the production of others. When a particular gene is active, it means that the body is allowing for the protein encoded by that gene to be produced. This applies to the immune system because the production of its cells and proteins, such as cytokines, depends on certain genes being active. As a result, seasonal differences in gene expression lead to differences in how the immune system functions.

To investigate this more closely, Dopico et al. (2015) tested whether genes like BMAL1, a gene that is known to follow a circadian rhythm, also follow an infradian rhythm, specifically aligned with the seasons. Instead of running an experiment themselves, the researchers analyzed large existing datasets of blood samples from people around the world. The analysis showed that about a quarter of the tested genes changed their expression seasonally. To further affirm that the finding was seasonal, the researchers tested blood samples from the northern hemisphere and the southern hemisphere separately and found that the shifts in gene expression were reversed, which indicates that the gene expressions matched local seasons. Researchers also observed that in the wintertime, immune-related genes shifted towards a more pro-inflammatory state which is represented by a higher number of monocytes, the white blood cell involved in inflammation, lower activity of BMAL1, which is known to suppress inflammation, and higher levels of proteins that are produced in response to cytokine firing. These changes suggest a more reactive immune system in the winter, possibly because the body evolved to prepare for the higher number of infections during that season.

The variation of the immune system is not solely represented by gene expression. Liu and Taioli (2015) aimed to provide a large-scale baseline showing that the immune system is not stagnant throughout the seasons. Using CDC survey data with blood counts from surveys between the years 1999 and 2012, they found that white blood cells and neutrophils, cells that play a part in inflammation, were also higher in the winter and spring than in the summer and fall. Moreover, this difference was stronger in children than adults, which the authors suggest may be because a developing immune system is more sensitive to seasonal changes. The researchers also suggest that this more inflammatory winter state may help the body defend against the colds and flu that are common during those months. Together with the findings discussed earlier, it is evident that the immune system not only depends on time of day, but also time of year.
